372.title: My own size
372.hook: take a role beyond your powers and you fail it and neglect the one you could have filled (Enchiridion 37)
372.carry: the part that really was yours
372.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review their commitments and decline roles beyond their present powers, to protect the roles they already hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was banquet, and the biggest portion that loses its value at a shared table. Your line was for the sake of the fellowship.

The email says: we were hoping you'd chair the committee. You're flattered. You're also already behind on everything, you've never run a budget, and the committee meets on the night you usually put your kids to bed. You say yes anyway. Six months later the committee is struggling, and so is bedtime. Section thirty-seven of the handbook is a single sentence, and it names both things that went wrong.
screen: `WE HOPED YOU'D CHAIR THE COMMITTEE.` → `YOU SAY YES ANYWAY.` → `MY OWN SIZE.`

segments.voice: If you take on a role beyond your powers, Epictetus says, you disgrace yourself in it, and you neglect the role you could have filled. Two losses, not one. The Greek for role is prosōpon. It meant a face, then an actor's mask, then the part the mask stood for. Back in section seventeen you met this picture: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote, and your job is to play your part well. Today adds the other side: don't grab a part that isn't yours. Latin used persona for the same idea, mask and role together, and Cicero, drawing on an earlier Stoic, built a whole theory of the roles each person plays. Now the double cost. The first loss is obvious: the role you weren't ready for goes badly, and people see it. The second is quieter and usually bigger. The part that really was yours, the friend, the parent, the craftsman, the neighbor, gets the leftovers. Nobody throws a party for a role you neglected. It just thins out. What this isn't: a rule to stay small forever. In a couple of weeks the handbook will ask, sharply, how long you're going to wait to become your best. Growth is welcome. The point is honesty about your present size: what you can carry now, what you're for right now, and which yes would cost a part you've already been given.

segments.voice: Think of what you've said yes to lately, the invitations, the asks, the jobs you took because nobody else would, and find one that's beyond your powers right now, or keeps eating time from a part that's really yours. Don't solve it; just name it. Then picture saying, kindly and clearly, I'm not the right person for this, and notice what loosens.

Your line: the part that really was yours. Every yes spends a little of it. Day three hundred seventy-two, done.

373.title: Mind the step
373.hook: as you watch for nails when walking, watch over your ruling mind (Enchiridion 38)
373.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use slow, attentive walking as a reminder to pause before accepting a judgment, guarding the mind as carefully as their footing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prosōpon, a role. Take one beyond your powers and two parts suffer. Your line was the part that really was yours.

Walk barefoot across a garage floor and watch what happens to you. Nobody has to tell you to pay attention. Your eyes go to every step. Your weight hangs back for a beat before each foot lands, just in case there's a nail, a screw, a sharp bit of glass. You do it without thinking, because you know what a nail in the foot feels like. Section thirty-eight of the handbook takes that ordinary carefulness and points it somewhere new.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON A GARAGE FLOOR.` → `EVERY STEP WATCHED.` → `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: Just as when you walk you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot, Epictetus says, take care in the same way not to harm your ruling mind. If you watched for this in every action, you'd go about each one more safely. The Greek is hēgemonikon, the ruling part. It's related to hēgemōn, a leader or guide. For the Stoics, the hēgemonikon was the command center of a person, where impressions are received, judged, and given or refused assent. Chrysippus, one of the school's early heads, even placed it in the heart. Marcus Aurelius uses the word again and again in his private notebook. Notice how much care you already give the body without effort. You watch for nails, wipe up spills, check the stairs in the dark. Epictetus asks for the same easy care for the part of you that decides. What does a nail look like for the mind? A judgment made in a rush. A resentment you agree to without checking. An impression, he's rude, I'm a failure, it's ruined, accepted at face value. Each one is a small injury to the ruling part, and like a foot injury, it changes how you walk for a while afterward. The fix isn't fear. It's attention at the moment of stepping: a beat before agreeing to the thought, the way you hang back before your foot lands.

Hēgemonikon. The Stoic word for the ruling part of the mind, where impressions are judged. Guard it, Epictetus says, as you guard your feet. Today's word.
Your line: a beat before agreeing. The ruling part deserves the care your feet already get. That's day three hundred seventy-three.

374.title: The foot measures the shoe
374.hook: the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe (Enchiridion 39)
374.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use the body's actual needs as a measure for buying and owning, and notice when a want has gone past what the body asks for.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hēgemonikon, the ruling mind, guarded like a foot on a garage floor. Your line was a beat before agreeing.

Open a closet and count the shoes. Not to judge. Just count. Then count your feet. Two, for most people. Somewhere between those two numbers there's a story. A pair for running. Then a nicer pair for running. Then a pair that matches the jacket. Epictetus, who by tradition lived with very little, looked at the humble shoe and saw a whole philosophy of having. Section thirty-nine is short.
screen: `COUNT THE SHOES.` → `NOW COUNT YOUR FEET.` → `THE FOOT MEASURES THE SHOE.`

segments.voice: The body, Epictetus says, is the measure of what each person needs to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. A shoe has a job, and the foot tells you when it's done. Food, clothing, shelter: the body tells you, roughly, how much is enough. Stop there, he says, and you'll keep the measure. Step past it, and you'll be carried along as if over a cliff. Past the measure, there's no natural place to stop. He tells the slide with a shoe. Once you go beyond what the foot needs, the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered. Hear the ladder in those three words: plain leather becomes a show. Each step makes sense once you've taken the one before it, and nothing on the ladder ever says that's enough. Why is the body such a good measure? It comes with you. It doesn't read advertisements. It gets full, it gets warm, it gets dry, and then it's done. Desire has no such signal. Epicurus, who led a rival school, made a similar point in his own way: what nature needs is limited and easy to get, while what empty opinion wants has no limit. Two schools, each with its own reasons, pointing at the same quiet fact. Enough is a real thing.

375.title: Honor the character
375.hook: girls flattered for looks from fourteen should learn they're honored for self-respect (Enchiridion 40)
375.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism make a habit of praising others, especially children, for character and effort rather than appearance, following Epictetus' point in Enchiridion 40.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epicurus, and the shoe that slides from gilded to purple to embroidered. Your line was the foot measures.

Listen to what grown-ups say to children at a family party. To the little boys: you're so strong, you're so fast. To the little girls, again and again: look how pretty you are. It's meant kindly. But children pick up what the adults around them value, often from exactly these small remarks. Epictetus noticed the same thing in his own world, and wrote it down in a section of the handbook that's short, a little uncomfortable, and still sharp.
screen: `STRONG, FAST. PRETTY.` → `CHILDREN LEARN WHAT WE VALUE.` → `HONOR THE CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: In section forty, Epictetus says that from about fourteen, girls are flattered by men and called ladies. Seeing that they're valued for nothing except their appeal to men, he says, they begin to dress up and put all their hopes in that. His answer: it's worth taking care that they come to understand they're honored for nothing else than being decent and self-respecting. Not for looks. For character. That's the whole section. An honest note. It's written about girls, by a man, in a society that gave women little say over their own lives, and some modern readers find parts of its framing dated. But the core sentence points a finger at the people doing the flattering as much as at the girls, and it says plainly that a young woman's worth is in her character. Stoic teachers before him, like Musonius Rufus, Epictetus' own teacher, argued that women should study philosophy too. Why it reaches us: the praise people give teaches others what they're worth. Praise only looks, and you teach someone to put their hopes in a mirror, which time will eventually disappoint. Praise honesty, kindness, courage, effort, and you point them at the part of themselves nobody can take away. In Stoic terms, you praise what's up to them. That works for boys, for adults, for anyone.

376.title: Mind first
376.hook: spending too long on the body is a sign of neglecting the mind (Enchiridion 41)
376.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep the body's routines simple and set aside a few deliberate minutes each day for reading, reflection or journaling.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Musonius Rufus, and praise that honors character over looks. Your line was nobody can take away.

Add it up for one ordinary day. The workout. The shower and the hair. The meals, the snacks, the planning of meals. The skincare, the mirror, the step count on the watch. Now add up the minutes that went to the mind on purpose: thinking something through, reading something that stretched you, asking whether a judgment was true. Which list is longer? Epictetus doesn't ask you to drop the first one. He asks you to look at the ratio.
screen: `ADD UP THE BODY'S MINUTES.` → `NOW THE MIND'S.` → `MIND FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's a sign of a dull nature, Epictetus says, to spend a lot of time on the things of the body: a lot of exercise, a lot of eating, a lot of drinking, and the rest of the body's business. The key words are a lot. He isn't against the body. His own teacher, Musonius Rufus, taught that students should train the body as well as the soul, through cold and heat and hard work. Epictetus doesn't forbid eating, drinking or exercise either. He asks you to notice when the body's business takes up the whole day. These things, he says, should be done in passing, along the way. All your care should turn toward the mind. The Greek here is gnōmē, a word for judgment, outlook, the way a person thinks things through. For the Stoics, that's where a life actually gets lived: in how you judge what happens. A well-tended body with a neglected mind is like a beautifully kept house where no one ever opens the windows. Why it's urgent: the body will be looked after whether you plan it or not. Hunger reminds you. Tiredness reminds you. Nothing in the day reminds you to think. The mind only gets its turn if you give it one on purpose. Not because the body doesn't matter, but because the mind is the one that gets forgotten.

377.title: It seemed right to him
377.hook: when someone wrongs you, remember he did what seemed right to him (Enchiridion 42)
377.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often remind themselves, when wronged, that the other person acted on what seemed right to them, which helps them respond without adding anger.

segments.voice: Yesterday's lesson was mind first: the body's business in passing, real care for the mind. Your line was open the windows.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, and in the half second before the horn, a whole story forms in your head about who they are. Selfish. Reckless. Probably like this all the time. Hardly anyone pauses to tell the other story: that from inside that car, the move made sense. Late for a shift. A kid crying in the back. A misjudged mirror. Or simply a belief that the lane was theirs. Section forty-two of the handbook asks you to tell that second story, every time.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `A WHOLE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.` → `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.`

segments.voice: When someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does it or says it because he thinks it's right for him to. He can't act on what seems right to you. Only on what seems right to him. If what seemed right to him is wrong, he's the one harmed, because he's the one who was deceived. Epictetus gives an example from logic: if someone takes a true statement to be false, the statement isn't harmed. The person who got it wrong is. The root is an idea often traced to Socrates, in Plato's dialogues: that nobody does wrong knowingly, believing it to be wrong. People act on what looks good to them, even when it isn't. The Stoics inherited that idea and built on it. So the person who wrongs you isn't a monster who chose evil. They're someone who saw it wrong. From here, Epictetus says, you'll be gentle with the one who insults you. And he gives a short phrase to say each time, only two words in his Greek, a little like a breath before reacting: it seemed so to him. That isn't an excuse for harm. You can still protect yourself, set a limit, even seek justice. What changes is the heat. You stop adding your own anger to their mistake. You see a person who judged badly, not an enemy. And that turns out to be lighter to carry.

For a minute, stand where they stood and ask what they believed was true, or fair, or necessary; you don't have to agree, just look. Then say quietly, it seemed right to him, or to her, or to them, and notice what happens to the heat.

Your line: lighter to carry. Two words can cool a lot of heat. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

378.title: The other handle
378.hook: everything has two handles; take your brother by "he is my brother," not "he wronged me" (Enchiridion 43)
378.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often reframe a conflict with someone close by starting from the relationship rather than the offense, following Epictetus' image of the two handles.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Socrates, and the idea that nobody does wrong knowingly. Your line was lighter to carry.

A pot on the stove has two handles. One has been sitting over the flame, and it's scorching. The other is cool. Grab the hot one and you drop the pot, and now there's soup on the floor and a burn on your hand. Nobody would blame the pot. You just picked it up by the wrong side. Section forty-three of the Enchiridion is about that choice, and Epictetus aims it straight at family.
screen: `A POT WITH TWO HANDLES.` → `ONE HOT, ONE COOL.` → `THE OTHER HANDLE.`

segments.voice: Everything has two handles, Epictetus says: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. The pot is today's picture, not his, but the handles are his. If your brother wrongs you, he says, don't take hold of it by the handle he wronged me. That's the handle by which it can't be carried. Take it by the other one: he's my brother, we were raised together. Then you'll be holding it by the handle that can be carried. The wrong still happened; Epictetus doesn't pretend otherwise. What changes is which fact you pick up first. Grab he wronged me, and every other fact arranges itself around the injury. Grab he's my brother, and the injury becomes one fact inside a longer story, a story with a shared childhood and a kitchen table and probably a few wrongs going the other way. Same situation, different handle, different weight. It works beyond brothers. A coworker, a neighbor, a parent, a friend who let you down. Each relationship has its own cool handle: she's been loyal for ten years. He's my father. We've built this together. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: my own size. Mind the step. The foot measures. Honor the character. Mind first. It seemed right to him. Yesterday and today belong together: first you see why they did it, then you choose how to hold it.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAS TWO HANDLES.` · `NOT 'HE WRONGED ME.' 'HE'S MY BROTHER.'` · `SAME FACTS, DIFFERENT WEIGHT.` · `EVERY RELATIONSHIP HAS A COOL HANDLE.` · then, large: `THE OTHER HANDLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conflict you're carrying with someone close, and notice which handle you've been holding it by: what they did, what they said, how hot it is. Then gently look for the other handle: who they are to you, what you've shared, what's true about them besides this. Pick the whole thing up by that one fact, and notice the difference in weight.
Two handles, Epictetus says everything has: one that can be carried, and one that can't. Pick up your brother by the one that can. Today's word.
Your line: he's my brother. The cool handle is often the older story. Day three hundred seventy-eight, and another week done.
